$comment: Observability retention, sampling, queue bounds, and taxonomy. Not a UI knob. Missing required keys fail boot. Never put secrets here.
_memoryTelemetryComment: Readiness pass (2026-09-04): a durable (persisted, not in-memory-only) memory sample on a much coarser cadence than processTelemetryIntervalMs, specifically so a future silent death has real Argus-side memory-trend history to examine instead of relying on Windows' own external resource-exhaustion detector (the only evidence available for the Sept 2-3 deaths). Thresholds are evidence-labeled, not asserted precise: warning=2048MB sits above every healthy Node RSS baseline observed this session (600-800MB in the first 30-60min); critical=3584MB sits just under the ~3.85GB Node RSS peak that immediately preceded a prior silent death - close enough to alert before reaching that exact danger zone, not a proven safe ceiling. Recalibrate once a full RTH session's real Node memory curve (post Chronos-leak-fix) exists.
_memoryTelemetryCommittedComment: Readiness audit (2026-09-04) found the RSS thresholds above structurally CANNOT see the real Chronos failure mode on this Windows host. Measured live: the sidecar held 15,245.9MB of pagefile/commit charge and 6,451 OS threads while reporting 469.9MB working set - Windows had trimmed the working set, so this sampler had recorded level=NORMAL for hours against a process consuming ~30% of the host's ~50.9GB commit limit. Crucially, that instance had served ZERO inferences (/health lastInferenceMs was null), so commit growth of this shape is NOT explained by the torch.inference_mode() autograd-retention fix alone - thread accumulation in ThreadingHTTPServer is the larger contributor and remains open. These thresholds therefore watch COMMITTED memory (psutil memory_info().vms - pagefile charge on Windows, virtual size on POSIX) via the new numeric /health field committedMemoryMb. HONESTY: no committed-memory baseline for a FRESHLY started, healthy Chronos+FinBERT has been measured yet, so both numbers are provisional bounds chosen from the degraded measurement, not a calibrated healthy range - warning=6144MB and critical=12288MB both sit below the observed 15,245.9MB and leave real headroom under the commit limit. Expect the currently-running (degraded) sidecar to report CRITICAL immediately; that is the intended behaviour. Re-derive both once a fresh restart's real curve exists.
_heapSnapshotComment: P1-A memory-leak investigation (2026-09-14, ~29MB/min sustained linear RSS growth over a 112-minute session, root cause unidentified after static code review ruled out several bounded collections) is a SEPARATE, still-unresolved incident from P1-B below - the diagnostic built to investigate P1-A itself became a second, confirmed reliability hazard; do not conflate the two. P1-B, CONFIRMED (not suspected): the first live WARNING-level capture (pid 27000, 2026-09-14T20:17:52Z) was followed by the engine's event loop going unresponsive for ~6 minutes (watchdog.log: heartbeat staleness climbing continuously from 20:18:28Z, FROZEN_CONFIRMED + external force-kill at 20:24:10Z) - the process being killed by the watchdog is a directly observed fact, not an inference. LIKELY MECHANISM (well-supported by timing + a 2.04GB completed output file + the missing completion log, but not proven to the level of an exact duration-vs-size formula): v8.writeHeapSnapshot() is a real, synchronous, unavoidably-blocking V8 heap walk; serializing ~2.04GB is consistent with a multi-minute block. Do not claim more precision than this evidence supports. Baseline captures at low (~600MB) heap measured 8.8-11.8s on two occasions - this shows baseline capture has been safe UNDER THAT SPECIFIC TESTED CONDITION, not that it is intrinsically or generally event-loop-safe at arbitrary heap sizes; two low-memory data points do not extrapolate to a multi-GB heap. CORRECTION (2026-09-15, post-forensic-audit): the claim below that baseline-only capture 'remains enabled as a narrowly-scoped exception' is STALE and WRONG - captureHeapSnapshot()/scheduleBaselineHeapSnapshot()/maybeCaptureHeapSnapshotForMemoryLevel() (heapSnapshotCapture.ts) are ALL gated by this SAME single heapSnapshotEnabled flag, which is currently false - baseline capture is therefore ALSO currently disabled, not a narrowly-scoped exception to the elevated-level disable below. Both WARNING/CRITICAL-triggered AND baseline capture are off pending the genuine process-level-separation redesign described below; re-enabling either requires flipping this one flag back to true, which reintroduces the exact synchronous-freeze risk for both. IMPORTANT for any future redesign: this is not fixable by wrapping the same synchronous call in a Promise/setImmediate/same-process worker - v8.writeHeapSnapshot() blocks the calling thread's own event loop regardless of how that call is scheduled, and a worker_thread has its own separate V8 heap (it cannot snapshot the main thread's heap by being asked nicely from within the same process). A real fix requires the trading-critical process to never be the one whose heap gets synchronously walked - i.e. genuine process-level separation between the trading-critical process and any research/forensic process that needs deep heap introspection, not a same-process async-looking wrapper. Preserved for that future design: the mechanism's original scoping (baseline snapshot shortly after boot, one snapshot at the first WARNING/CRITICAL transition, one optional follow-up, a hard per-process-lifetime cap, disk-bounded pruning) and duration logging on every capture. Never gates or delays MemoryTelemetryGuard's own TRADING_PAUSED intervention.
_heavyReportGuardComment: Trading/research-plane isolation (2026-09-14, item #25 / mandate Phase 2). Real incident: a heavy diagnostic HTTP call (argus-cli strategy-fairness) against the live engine is the leading suspected trigger for that same day's process crash - no proof of exact mechanism, but real enough to require a structural guard, not just caution. Applies to the heaviest read-only observability reports (agent-edge, strategy-fairness, strategy-scorecard - each does a real, non-trivial scan over potentially tens of thousands of rows). Two real protections: (1) serialized - only one heavy report may run at a time, preventing exactly the pile-up pattern the incident showed; (2) a memory circuit breaker reusing memoryTelemetryWarningRssMb (no new duplicate threshold) - refuses to even start a heavy report while RSS is already at/above WARNING, the exact precondition present during the incident. heavyReportTimeoutMs bounds how long a CALLER waits, not the underlying synchronous SQLite work itself (Node cannot forcibly cancel that once started) - the guard's mutex stays held until the real work actually finishes, honestly modeling this limitation rather than pretending to cancel it.
